analysis.one_liner: Repeals federal fuel-economy standards that set how far cars must go on a gallon of gas.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced: introduced with zero cosponsors, it was sent to the Energy and Commerce Committee and died there when the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This one-page bill would wipe out the corporate average fuel economy (CAFE) standards, the federal rules requiring automakers to build vehicle fleets that travel a set average distance per gallon of fuel. Without those standards, automakers would be free to sell whatever mix of vehicles they choose. Repeal would tend to push new-car buyers toward vehicles that burn more gasoline, raising fuel spending for households and increasing oil consumption and emissions.
analysis.who_benefits: Automakers, which would no longer face the engineering and compliance costs of meeting fuel-economy targets, and sellers of gasoline, which would see demand rise as vehicle efficiency declines. Some buyers of large vehicles might see sticker prices fall relative to a world with strict standards.

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals Chapter 329 of title 49, U.S. Code, the statutory basis of the corporate average fuel economy standards, eliminating the requirement that automakers' fleets meet a mandated average miles-per-gallon level [S3].
The CRS summary states plainly that the bill repeals the standards that regulate how far automobiles must travel on a gallon of fuel [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Drivers, who would spend more on gasoline over the life of each vehicle as average fuel economy stops improving; and the public more broadly, through higher gasoline consumption and the associated emissions. Households in the market for a new vehicle would face a thinner supply of efficient options.

drawbacks.text: Repeal would end decades of steadily improving fleet fuel economy, leaving consumers with no federal floor on efficiency and higher long-run fuel costs [S2].

A good-faith argument for repeal is that fuel-economy mandates add to the price of new vehicles and can force automakers to prioritize small cars over vehicles some buyers want; the bill's sponsor offered it to eliminate those rules entirely [S3]. But the bill takes an all-or-nothing approach, removing the standards rather than adjusting their stringency, and no other member signed on.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit is hypothetical savings on new-vehicle sticker prices for automakers' customers and reduced compliance costs for manufacturers. The cost falls on every driver through higher fuel use over the life of each vehicle, plus higher emissions. Because repeal is total rather than a recalibration of stringency, the fuel-cost burden on households is large and ongoing, and it outweighs the one-time vehicle-price effect for most families.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which referred it to a subcommittee, and it never came to a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Roger Williams introduced the bill on January 10, 2019 [S1].
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce [S5].
On January 25, 2019, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Consumer Protection and Commerce, and no further action was taken for the rest of the Congress [S5].
No other member cosponsored the bill [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Automakers gained nothing, since the standards remain in force; drivers and the public keep the fuel-economy rules the bill would have repealed.

for.name: Rep. Roger Williams
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the CAFE standards.

against.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to a subcommittee on January 25, 2019 and never scheduled a markup or floor action; the bill died in committee.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was a one-member Republican effort with zero cosponsors in a Democratic-controlled House, and it never reached a vote, so no recorded partisan vote exists.

industries.note: Repeal would free automakers from fuel-economy compliance costs, but the savings would come at the expense of drivers, who would pay more for fuel over each vehicle's life. The bill's benefit to the industry runs against the public's interest in efficient vehicles.
Weaker fuel-economy standards mean more gasoline burned per mile, increasing demand for refiners and fuel retailers. That gain comes directly out of household fuel budgets.
